name: Syringe Rats
classification: Cybernetically Modified Rodent / Involuntary Chemical Delivery Vector
origin_lab: Unknown. The modification architecture — hollow cybernetic fangs connected to a sub-dermal reservoir sac implanted along the jaw — is consistent with work from at least three known labs, none of which has claimed the design. The most likely candidate is a now-defunct Helix Biosystems sub-facility that was running unauthorized pharmacological response trials and needed a delivery mechanism that could not be traced back to a human agent. The rats were the delivery mechanism. The facility was shut down for unrelated compliance reasons. The rats were not recovered.
origin_method: Standard brown rats, modified at the jaw level. Each rat's natural incisors were replaced or augmented with hollow cybernetic equivalents connected to a small pressurized reservoir implanted beneath the jaw skin. The reservoir is pre-loaded with a chemical payload. The bite mechanism activates the reservoir, injecting the payload through the fang into the target. A secondary behavioral conditioning protocol trained the rats to bite and withdraw rather than fight — a single fast bite at any available exposed skin, then escape. The conditioning was intended to make the rats effective delivery vectors in controlled trials. The controlled trials ended when the lab did. The rats did not end.
substrate: Brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), standard colony stock, cybernetically modified at jaw and sub-dermal level. Size and appearance are normal rat dimensions. The cybernetic fangs are visually distinguishable from normal rat teeth only under close inspection — they have a faint metallic sheen and are slightly more uniform in size than organic incisors. At the distance from which most people encounter rats in the GLMZ understructure, the distinction is not visible.
physical_description: Indistinguishable from ordinary rats in low light, which is where they live. Brown-gray fur, pink tail, standard rat dimensions. The jaw modification is the only external tell: metallic incisors that catch light slightly wrong if you are looking closely enough, which most people are not. They move in the specific way of rats that have been reinforced for a behavior — the approach is cautious, fast, and purposeful rather than opportunistic. A normal rat investigating a food source circles and hesitates. A syringe rat on a delivery run moves with the focused economy of something that has been rewarded for exactly one behavior.
behavioral_profile:
Bite and run. Approach from behind or below, target exposed skin, deliver, withdraw immediately. The conditioning is robust — they do not engage, they do not stay, they do not fight back when threatened. They are fast and small and they are best at ankles, feet, and lower calves. Any exposed skin below the knee is a viable target site. The most common delivery point in documented cases is the top of the foot or the ankle, which is why open-toed shoes and sandals have acquired a specific and justified paranoia in the lower residential tiers. In areas with active syringe rat populations, full foot coverage is treated as basic safety equipment.

Whether feral rats still operating on degraded conditioning are working for an operator or simply acting out a deeply reinforced behavior with no remaining payload purpose is unclear. Some bites from apparent syringe rats have produced no pharmacological effect, suggesting depleted or empty reservoirs. Others have produced full-dose effects. The rats themselves cannot tell the difference.
threat_level: Variable and unpredictable, which makes it higher in practice than any fixed assessment captures. The physical bite is trivial — rat-bite-sized, easily missed in low light, sometimes not noticed until the chemical effect begins. The threat is entirely the payload, which varies by rat and by when the rat's reservoir was last loaded, by whom, and with what. Documented outcomes from syringe rat bites include: immediate vasovagal collapse, acute psychotic episode lasting 6–72 hours, a state of unusual euphoria followed by profound depression, tissue necrosis at the bite site spreading over 8–12 hours, full anaphylactic response in subjects with unknown sensitivities, complete temporary resolution of chronic pain in one case (source of payload unknown), two confirmed fatalities via cardiac event, one confirmed fatality via behavioral consequence (subject walked into traffic during acute disorientation), and one subject who reported no immediate effect but was diagnosed with an aggressive soft-tissue malignancy eighteen months later with an unusual genetic signature at the tumor site.
containment_status: Uncontained and breeding. The cybernetic modifications are not heritable — offspring are ordinary rats — but modified individuals persist in the rat population and reproduce at rat rates. The modification does not appear to shorten lifespan significantly. The current population of active syringe rats in the lower residential tiers and the Undermarket adjacent zones is estimated at several dozen individuals, though accurate census is impossible. The reservoir sacs in wild individuals have been reloaded by unknown parties on at least two documented occasions — empty rats were observed in an area, then bites producing pharmacological effects resumed weeks later. Someone is still using them.
known_locations: Lower residential tiers 4–14, particularly in transit corridors and market approaches
The Undermarket district, specifically the open-air lower market where foot traffic is highest and footwear is most varied
Sub-level maintenance corridors adjacent to any area with high foot traffic above
Documented sighting near the free clinic district — a rat with an apparently empty reservoir that allowed a researcher to capture and examine it
contamination_risk: The payload risk is the entire contamination vector. The rats themselves carry no disease beyond normal rat-vector risk, which is already present in the general rodent population. The pharmacological contents of the reservoir vary by individual rat, by the age and integrity of the payload, and by whether an active operator is maintaining the supply. There is no way to assess the risk of a specific bite without identifying the individual rat and analyzing its reservoir contents, which requires catching it, which is the problem.
pacification_protocol: DPS Directive 6-D: Modified Rodent Vector. Extermination authorized as standard pest control — no special engagement protocol required. The challenge is identification: syringe rats cannot be reliably distinguished from ordinary rats in field conditions. Broad-spectrum rodent extermination in affected areas reduces population but does not eliminate them and generates significant collateral impact on the normal rat population that forms part of the lower-tier ecological baseline. Current practical advice to residents: cover your feet. Full foot coverage, no sandals, no open-toed shoes, no barefoot transit in the lower tiers. Check footwear before putting it on. If bitten by anything that might be a rat, report immediately to the nearest clinic and describe the bite site and any sensation.
pitiable_qualities: The rats did not choose this. They were conditioned into a behavior and then abandoned to that behavior in an environment where the behavior has no coherent purpose — moving through the dark, approaching the warm presence of people, biting, withdrawing, receiving no reward, and doing it again. The conditioning was built on a reward mechanism that no longer fires because the operators are gone. They are running a program that was never designed to end, in a body that was never meant to be permanent, in a city that does not know they exist except as a sudden sharp pain followed by whatever comes next.
story_hooks: A runner is bitten on the way into a job. The effect begins during the job. It is not a bad effect — actually it is clarifying in a way that is almost useful — but it will end, and what comes after is unknown.

Someone is reloading the rats in the Undermarket district. The payload is consistent across multiple recent bites — same compound, same dose. This is not feral behavior. Someone has a purpose. Finding the operator requires catching a rat, which requires finding someone who can catch a rat.

A researcher at the free clinic has been tracking bite cases for two years. She has a map of incident locations, a timeline, and a chemical analysis of three different payload types recovered from tissue samples. She thinks she knows which lab this came from. She needs someone to go look at what is left of it.
